title: SRE postmortem + runbook draft: customer egress-policy throttle -> control-plane reachability
content:
Summary:

Short version: customer deployed a restrictive egress policy and an automated traffic-shaping rule in their on-prem environment which intermittently prevented our control-plane health-check and metric ingestion endpoints from being reachable. Result: degraded management plane (rollouts, metrics, crash reporting) for that customer for ~2.5 hours. Control-plane (data path) for inference remained OK for most traffic because traffic to model endpoints used a separate allowed path.

Impact:
- Time window: 2025-02-11 04:12 UTC -> 2025-02-11 06:42 UTC (approx)
- Symptoms: missing heartbeats in Console, failed canary rollouts, increased agent restart loops, customer reported failing admin UI and slow metric updates.
- Scope: single customer private deployment (vpc on-prem) behind customer-managed firewall and egress gateway.
- Severity: Sev2 (management plane degraded, inference largely unaffected).

How detected:
- Pager triggered by missing heartbeat aggregator alert (sre-heartbeat-missing) at 04:15 UTC
- Console team ticket created from internal alerting -> SRE on-call assigned
- Customer Slack: initial report that "admin UI shows control plane unreachable" at ~04:23 UTC

Initial triage notes (on-call):
- Checked global control-plane availability: green (hosted control plane healthy)
- Checked customer agent logs: agent reported 502/timeout errors when contacting https://controlplane.prod.redwood.ai/health-check
- Verified agent can resolve DNS for control plane but TLS handshake timed out intermittently
- Ran curl from customer agent container: many requests took >10s or timed out; some succeeded
- Observed packet drops on tcpdump: repeated RSTs and ICMP unreachable from gateway when outbound ports > 1024 were used

Timeline (key events):
- 04:12 UTC: first missed aggregation window; automated canary rollback failed
- 04:15 UTC: on-call alerted, started triage, requested customer contact point
- 04:20 UTC: customer ops confirms recent change: applied egress rate-limiter and tightened ephemeral port range to reduce NAT exhaustion (policy name: "egress-throttle-jan2025")
- 04:28 UTC: we reproduce timeout patterns from agent host using wget/curl -> find port-dependent failures
- 04:50 UTC: temporary mitigation suggested: ask customer to add explicit allow for control-plane IP prefix and allow ephemeral port range 1024-65535 (customer reluctant about broad range)
- 05:10 UTC: customer tries adding specific IPs; still intermittent -> likely ephemeral NAT / connection tracking timeout + rate-limit interacting with short-lived TLS sessions
- 05:40 UTC: customer increases egress connection tracking table and relaxes rate limit rules -> immediate improvement in success rate
- 06:42 UTC: telemetry stable, alert cleared, follow-up actions created

Root cause analysis (probable):
- The customer had a firewall/egress gateway rule that limited concurrent/outbound new connections per-second and narrowed ephemeral port allocation to 40000-40100 to control NAT usage. This caused TLS connection churn (many short-lived connections for control-plane heartbeats and metrics) to be rate-limited and some connections to be actively dropped by the gateway (RSTs/ICMP).
- Additionally, connection tracking table size on the gateway was low and entries were being recycled aggressively, causing SYN/ACK races for new ephemeral ports.
- Because our control-plane uses short-lived HTTPS connections per control message (no long-lived TCP in that deployment), bursts of control-plane traffic were more sensitive to ephemeral port and connection limits than the inference data path (which used persistent proxies).

Mitigations performed during incident:
- On-call recommended customer add explicit egress allows for control-plane CIDR block (we provided list) and to widen the ephemeral source port range to 1024-65535 temporarily.
- Customer increased connection-tracking table size and relaxed per-second new-connection limit.
- We toggled agent backoff to be less aggressive so that failures didn't spin the agent restart loop (temporary config pushed via remote management).
- Validation: after changes, heartbeat success rate rose to normal within ~30 minutes.

Permanent fixes and action items (owners + ETA):
- SRE (Aisha): draft a short-runbook for private deployments describing minimal egress requirements for control plane (CIDRs, ports, ephemeral port recommendations) — ETA 2025-02-18.
- Product (Priya): add explicit note in Private deployment quickstart and onboarding checklist about NAT/egress settings and recommended conntrack values — ETA 2025-03-01.
- Eng-Serving (Marco): investigate support for persistent control plane connections (WebSocket/HTTP2) in the agent to reduce TLS churn in NAT-restricted environments — spike by 2025-03-10.
- SRE (Liam): create monitoring checks that detect port-dependent transient errors (count of RSTs/ICMP from customer gateways) and flag potential conntrack saturation — ETA 2025-02-28.
- Customer Success: schedule a runthrough with top-10 enterprise customers who use on-prem/VPC installs to review egress recommendations — ETA 2025-03-15.

Runbook draft (for on-call dealing with similar incidents) — quick reference:
1) Detection:
   - Pager on missing heartbeats / control-plane 5xxs from agents
   - Console shows "agent disconnected" + agent log snippets contain TLS timeout / connection reset
2) First steps (0-15 min):
   - Confirm global control plane is healthy (status.redwood.ai / hosted metrics)
   - Collect agent logs (journalctl /var/log/redwood-agent.log) and last 100 lines
   - From agent host, run: curl -v --tlsv1.2 https://controlplane.prod.redwood.ai/health-check  (note timings)
   - Run tcpdump: sudo tcpdump -n -i <iface> host CONTROL_PLANE_IP and capture 60s -> look for RST, ICMP unreachable, SYN retransmits
   - Check agent DNS resolution and TLS cert validity
3) Triage checks (15-40 min):
   - Does issue differ by destination port? Try forcing source ports with socat (if allowed) or test from different hosts behind same gateway
   - Ask customer: recent firewall/egress changes? names of policy and exact rules
   - Ask customer to check NAT ephemeral port pool and conntrack table sizes (iptables -L -v -n, /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max)
   - If conntrack/isolation is suspected, ask to temporarily widen ephemeral port range and relax new-connection-per-second limits for the CIDR
4) Short-term mitigation (30-90 min):
   - Recommend explicit allow for control-plane IP prefixes and ports 443, 8443 (if using alternate)
   - Suggest using persistent proxy (customer side) to multiplex agent control traffic through fewer connections
   - As last resort, schedule a brief window to relax egress rules for rollout windows
5) Post-mitigation validation:
   - Confirm heartbeat frequency normalizes for 3 consecutive windows
   - Confirm agent logs show healthy TLS handshakes and no RSTs/ICMP unreachable
   - Update incident ticket and set follow-up tasks
6) Escalation:
   - If customer cannot relax egress rules: escalate to Eng-Serving to implement persistent control channel or backoff changes; consider temporary bypass via VPN for management plane.

Commands & diagnostic snippets (keep in runbook):
- curl with timing: time curl -w "\nhttp_code:%{http_code} time_total:%{time_total} time_connect:%{time_connect}\n" -o /dev/null -s https://controlplane.prod.redwood.ai/health-check
- tcpdump capture: sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 host <CONTROL_PLANE_IP> and "(tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-rst) != 0) or icmp" -w /tmp/cp-issue.pcap
- conntrack list/top: sudo conntrack -L | head -n 200
- check conntrack max: cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max || cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_conntrack_max
- ephemeral range check (customer): sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range
- temporary socat to test source port (if customer allows): sudo socat - TCP:controlplane.prod.redwood.ai:443,sourceport=40010,connect-timeout=5

Open questions / notes to follow up (notes to self):
- Need canonical control-plane IP prefix list that we maintain and publish to customers (avoid ad-hoc IP lists) -> depends on hosted infra changes.
- Consider adding an agent config option to prefer HTTP2 persistent control channel for management traffic (reduces churn).
- Investigate adding telemetry to detect per-customer RST/ICMP patterns automatically and trigger support playbook.
- Customer concern: security team did not want wide ephemeral range; need to prepare a minimal acceptable fallback (e.g., static NAT pool + persistent proxy recommendation).

Postmortem checklist (to complete before finalizing):
- [ ] Capture final timeline with exact timestamps from agent logs (Aisha)
- [ ] Confirm customer firewall rules and provide sanitized copy for internal postmortem (Customer Success)
- [ ] Publish runbook page in Confluence and link to onboarding docs (Priya)
- [ ] Create automated alert for conntrack saturation pattern (Liam)
- [ ] Decide on agent persistent-control-channel spike and scope (Marco)

Appendix: quick reference for egress recommendations (draft)
- Allow outbound to control-plane CIDR: 34.200.0.0/16, 52.41.0.0/16 (example placeholders; use canonical list)
- Allow outbound TCP ports: 443 (primary), 8443 (if configured)
- Make sure ephemeral source port range includes at least 1024-32767 or use static NAT pool that can route many simultaneous flows
- Conntrack table: ensure nf_conntrack_max sufficient for expected concurrent flows (rule of thumb: concurrent-flows * 4)
- Prefer a persistent agent control connection if customer policy prohibits wide ephemeral ranges

Notes to on-call rotation: keep this doc in mind when paging on "agent heartbeat" alerts. Private deployments commonly fail with network policy interactions rather than Redwood control-plane outages. When in doubt, first verify customer network/egress rules before scaling hosted infra.
